claims.Buyer_Implication: Class context is mandatory: Zoom's rational value can come from unified-stack simplicity and UX rather than maximum bespoke suite depth.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center qualifies as a core CCaaS platform and is best normalized in CLS-CC-004 Midmarket / unified-stack CCaaS rather than penalized against enterprise suites solely for a simplification-oriented architecture.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Fit rises for Zoom-standardized organizations and falls when the buyer needs a separate highly bespoke CCaaS control plane.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center serves growth, midmarket and enterprise buyers; its strongest structural fit is where Zoom Workplace/Phone familiarity and a consolidated operating experience reduce adoption and administration burden.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Sovereignty can improve at the cost of some global media-placement flexibility; exact regions must be validated.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Commercial Zoom Contact Center supports global SIP-zone coverage plus region-specific account models, but region-specific accounts can restrict use of SIP zones outside the selected region.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Federal qualification depends on ordering the exact Zoom for Government service and validating feature parity.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom for Government is a separate environment from commercial Zoom and includes a FedRAMP Moderate-authorized Zoom Contact Center service boundary; commercial and government capabilities/authorizations must not be silently inherited across environments.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Telephony flexibility is credible, but BYOC-P creates a shared support boundary with the customer/carrier.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center voice architecture supports Zoom-provided carrier connectivity and BYOC-P through customer-provided SBC/carrier integration.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Routing is materially deeper than Phase 1's basic-growth-platform shorthand.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center supports queue, skills, consumer-routing profiles, channel prioritization, intent routing, queue-data conditions and flow-based overflow/orchestration.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Large queue designs are supported, but buyer topology still needs construct-level sizing.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Current queue documentation allows up to 2,000 users per queue and configurable overflow/wait behavior.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Digital breadth is a validated strength and includes video as a distinctive native channel.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Current ZCC packaging supports inbound voice, video, chat and SMS in Essentials, with Premium adding email and social digital channels plus cobrowse and outbound.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Outbound is materially stronger than Phase 1's 2/5 shorthand, though predictive-dialing/compliance depth still requires use-case proof.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Premium ZCC includes outbound dialers; Zoom documents preview, progressive and agentless dialer modes.

claims.Buyer_Implication: The Phase 1 WFM maturity assessment is materially stale and should be reassessed upward after peer normalization.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Workforce Management now includes AI-powered shift scheduling, up to two years of historical-data retrieval, division support, intraday capabilities, projected-SLA reporting and overtime-board workflows.

claims.Buyer_Implication: QM is now a first-class native workforce capability rather than an immature add-on.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Quality Management supports manual and automated scorecards, coaching, automated-release controls and AI scoring.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Omnichannel QA buyers must not assume automated scoring has equal depth across channels.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Current automated QM scoring analyzes transcription content and does not currently auto-score email content.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Analytics breadth is current, but causal business-outcome claims still require buyer validation.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center provides live/operational reporting, Zoom CX Insights, QM/WFM analytics and expanding cross-CX insight surfaces.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Agent/supervisor workspace capability is materially more mature than the historical Phase 1 score.
claims.Publishable_Summary: The 2026 Zoom Contact Center agent workspace adds consumer, engagement and Zoom App workspaces, AI Expert Assist, CRM CTI integrations and cross-channel controls.

claims.Buyer_Implication: This can be a hard capability break for operations that require physical IP-phone agent handling.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center does not currently support IP phone compatibility for contact-center agents in the current technical overview.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Custom integration is credible and improving.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom exposes a broad Contact Center API v2 surface for engagements, flows, storage, campaigns, users, logs and administration.

claims.Buyer_Implication: API breadth does not equal unlimited integration throughput; high-volume designs need quota proof.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Contact Center APIs are subject to per-second and daily rate limits; Business+ examples include 40 light, 20 medium and 10 heavy requests per second with daily heavy limits.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Operational data access is strong, but full exit/portability must be contractually proven.
claims.Publishable_Summary: ZCC APIs expose storage-location and engagement data, and administrative operation logs can be exported to CSV; complete end-of-contract exportability across every CX module remains buyer-specific.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Architecture provides meaningful resilience evidence beyond marketing uptime statements.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center uses active-active architecture with two SIP zones per data center, redundant components and failover between SIP zones and data centers.

claims.Buyer_Implication: This is useful resilience/capacity evidence, but buyer-specific peak headroom still requires proof.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom states normal operations target no more than 50% capacity in each SIP zone so a failed zone can transfer load to the other zone.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Commercial security maturity is credible, while exact regulatory qualification remains service-bound.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom maintains broad commercial trust/compliance programs and supports Customer Managed Key for Zoom Contact Center; exact certification scope must be mapped to the proposed service.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Government qualification is strong when the correct service boundary is purchased.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom for Government Contact Center is FedRAMP Moderate authorized in a separate government environment.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Agent-assist maturity is materially stronger than Phase 1 captured.
claims.Publishable_Summary: AI Expert Assist provides real-time knowledge, recommendations, guidance, workflow assistance and wrap-up support; 2026 release notes document a next-generation agentic reasoning architecture.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Generation is broadly embedded, but generated output needs quality controls when consequential.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom AI surfaces generate summaries, smart notes, recommendations, evaluation output and analytical insights across ZCC/QM/Virtual Agent workflows.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Automation extends beyond conversational answers into workflow execution.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Virtual Agent and AI Expert Assist can automate multi-step customer-service workflows and tasks across integrated business systems.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Capability does not automatically earn unrestricted production authority.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Agent Architect/Zoom Virtual Agent is designed to reason, collaborate with other agents and orchestrate actions, so transactional authority must be bounded by tool permissions, confirmation, completion verification and rollback/compensation design.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Zoom now has credible current agentic-orchestration capability in the CX stack.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Agent Architect can create voice/digital AI agents from a prompt, coordinate multi-agent behavior and connect to Zoom CX context; Agent Performance Suite adds simulation and lifecycle optimization.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Model portability and inference locality are proof items for strategic-risk or sovereignty-sensitive buyers.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Public evidence reviewed does not establish unrestricted buyer model portability/BYOM across all Zoom CX AI features; AI engine/provider dependencies remain feature-specific and require buyer mapping.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Knowledge grounding is materially stronger than Phase 1's 2/5 shorthand, but content freshness and answer integrity must be tested.
claims.Publishable_Summary: AI Expert Assist and Zoom Virtual Agent use knowledge/context to ground recommendations and automated resolution; Agent Architect and customer-context enhancements strengthen cross-interaction grounding.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Governance surfaces exist, but high-consequence actions still require buyer-defined approval/incident controls.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom provides operation logs, AI-related admin controls, QM review workflows and shared quality evaluation across human and virtual-agent interactions.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Automation success and usage can change spend materially; the 'resolved' denominator must be contractually clear.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Virtual Agent introduced optional outcome-based pricing, while AI Expert Assist/Elite/other CX modules are quote-dependent; AI economics therefore require scenario-based TCO rather than seat-only comparison.

claims.Buyer_Implication: AI implementation gravity rises with action authority and business-system integration.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Production AI deployment requires knowledge preparation, test/simulation, integration/action design, quality evaluation, human fallback and ongoing performance monitoring.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Mainstream CRM/service-system fit is strong.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom Contact Center has current integrations across Salesforce, ServiceNow, Zendesk, Microsoft Dynamics 365, HubSpot, Salesforce Service Cloud Voice, Epic and ServiceNow Unified View.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Logo presence should not be treated as equal integration depth.
claims.Publishable_Summary: CRM integration depth varies by platform and channel; Zoom documents feature differences across connectors.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Support RACI must be explicit.
claims.Publishable_Summary: BYOC-P and CRM/custom integration create shared incident boundaries among Zoom, carrier, customer and third-party application owners.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Observable APIs improve supportability; failure behavior remains architecture-specific.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom operation logs, API/webhook patterns and explicit 429 behavior provide useful observability, but buyers still need fault-injection proof for CRM, API and carrier failures.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Custom API burden is contextual, not a universal platform weakness.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Packaged CRM connectors reduce custom work, while bespoke workflow/action logic, high-rate APIs and complex data synchronization can materially increase engineering burden.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Zoom can preserve a simplicity advantage only when the buyer does not overbuild the architecture.
claims.Publishable_Summary: A bounded Zoom Contact Center deployment can have LOW-to-MODERATE implementation gravity; gravity rises to HIGH for BYOC-P, multi-region sovereignty, complex migration, BPO divisions or transactional agentic AI.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Implementation speed claims are not portable across scopes.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Discovery must resolve corresponding Zoom license, telephony model, region/data policy, channel mix, WFM/QM, divisions, AI action scope and CRM/system-of-record ownership before effort is estimated.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Complex migrations require buyer-specific data/configuration conversion assessment.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom is cloud-native rather than a legacy-bridge architecture; public evidence reviewed does not establish a specialized automated migration factory for complex incumbent CCaaS estates.

claims.Buyer_Implication: A fast admin experience does not eliminate production-test burden.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Testing/UAT must cover routing, channels, CRM, telephony failover, WFM/QM, data locality, AI actions and endpoint behavior.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Unbounded discovery or product assumptions can convert simplicity into change orders.
claims.Publishable_Summary: SOW exposure concentrates in telephony/BYOC, migration, CRM customization, WFM/QM setup, divisions, AI action design, data/sovereignty and acceptance testing.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Implementation accelerators are useful, but old published service scopes are not current commitments.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom provides professional-services implementation options and a broad partner ecosystem; standard deployment can use packaged capabilities while larger programs still require architecture/migration expertise.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Day-2 ownership can remain comparatively business-admin friendly for standard designs.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Routine users, queues, flows, teams and WFM/QM administration can be owned by contact-center administrators; custom integration and AI action changes require more technical ownership.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Business operations can own substantial routing change without external services.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Queue, routing and flow changes are customer-administered, including overflow, channel prioritization, intent routing and data-table-driven decisions.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Day-2 workforce operations are increasingly native and internally operable.
claims.Publishable_Summary: WFM and QM expose native supervisor/admin workflows for schedules, forecasts, automated evaluation, release controls and coaching.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Technical-owner burden grows with customization and action authority.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Custom APIs, CRM workflows, BYOC-P and agentic actions require technical ownership and regression management.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Release velocity is an agility benefit and a change-management obligation.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom publishes frequent Contact Center, WFM, QM, Virtual Agent and CX Insights release notes, including staged/enablement-dependent features; buyers need release regression and feature-flag governance.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Observability is solid but cross-boundary troubleshooting remains an operating-model issue.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Operation logs, API error behavior, reporting and status tooling provide meaningful troubleshooting surfaces, while cross-provider BYOC and CRM incidents still require shared diagnostics.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Services dependency is scope-driven rather than intrinsic.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Standard Zoom CX deployments can keep professional-services dependency relatively low, while BYOC, custom integration, complex migration, BPO segmentation and high-authority AI increase specialist dependence.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Quote normalization is mandatory.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom currently publishes ZCC tier packaging but requires buyers to contact sales for numeric Essentials/Premium/Elite pricing; total platform cost depends on channels, WFM/QM, AI, telephony and corresponding Zoom licenses.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Platform simplicity does not guarantee low transformation cost in complex brownfield programs.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Transformation cost is likely low-to-moderate for greenfield Zoom-centric deployments but rises with carrier change, migration, CRM customization, division/BPO design, data controls and AI actions.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Run-state TCO should model human-seat and AI-outcome growth separately.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Run-state cost includes platform seats, telephony/usage, WFM/QM, AI Expert Assist/Virtual Agent, integration operations and customer administration; outcome-based ZVA pricing can add variable automation economics.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Seasonal/BPO buyers need explicit ramp, burst and AI-cost protections.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Because current public ZCC pricing is quote-based and AI can use outcome-based or module-specific economics, cost predictability depends on negotiated units, seasonality and automation growth.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Commercial flexibility should be negotiated rather than assumed.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Public evidence reviewed does not establish standardized true-down/ramp rights for ZCC; buyer-specific order terms must define seat flexibility, usage, renewal and module changes.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Zoom has stronger hard-isolation evidence than Phase 1 implied.
claims.Publishable_Summary: ZCX Divisions provide isolated environments for client brands/business units across ZCC, ZVA, WFM, QM and AI Expert Assist, with division-specific configurations and reports.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Isolation and shared-agent efficiency trade off directly.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Each user can belong to only one ZCX Division, so isolation can create a structural break for BPO shared-agent models that require one agent to work multiple clients/divisions concurrently.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Program launch can be efficient for dedicated-agent programs.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Divisions can accelerate separate-client program setup inside one account, but enabling the feature and duplicating division-specific objects introduces onboarding governance.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Dedicated-client operations fit better than highly shared-agent models.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Division-specific WFM, QM, queues, flows and reports support client separation, but shared-agent cross-division WEM/reporting is constrained by single-division user membership.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Margin management requires buyer proof of attribution/export.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Public documentation does not establish complete client-level attribution for platform, telephony, AI and other usage across BPO divisions.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Isolation is meaningful but not equivalent to physically independent accounts.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Divisions reduce cross-client configuration/data blast radius, but global admins and shared account/platform dependencies remain potential cross-division control points.

claims.Buyer_Implication: BPO commercial fit remains quote-dependent.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Commercial BPO flexibility is not sufficiently public to validate concurrent/shared-agent economics or true-down rights; the isolation model is clearer than the licensing model.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Where They Break is causal and buyer-condition specific.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom's primary causal breaks are required IP-phone agent endpoints; shared-agent BPO across isolated divisions; strict locality beyond supported region/account behavior; buyer topology/API capacity exceeding documented limits; and bespoke complexity that erodes unified-stack simplicity.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Exit/export obligations should be contractual.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Exitability is supported by APIs and exports for many operational datasets, but complete portability across recordings, WFM/QM, AI, configuration and interaction context is not fully established in public evidence.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Buyer fit is contextual and class-sensitive.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom fit rises with Zoom-estate consolidation, video-native CX, moderate operating capacity and fast cloud change; fit falls with desk-phone requirements, shared-agent BPO, strict bespoke orchestration or highly specialized legacy migration.

claims.Buyer_Implication: A demo is insufficient for production fit.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Material Zoom claims require buyer-controlled proof for peak capacity, division/BPO behavior, CRM failure, BYOC failover, automated QM validity, AI action integrity, data residency, endpoint fit and three-year economics.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Commercial and implementation safeguards are part of the product decision.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Contracts/SOWs should explicitly control service boundary, telephony responsibility, capacity, data/AI residency, AI pricing/action authority, WFM/QM scope, division/BPO assumptions, integration support, acceptance and data exit.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Unknowns increase proof burden without being encoded as weak capability.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Evidence confidence is high for current architecture, channels, WFM/QM, APIs, divisions, government authorization and 2026 AI releases; it is lower for buyer-specific capacity, full exitability, strict AI model locality and commercial true-down/usage economics.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Capacity is measurable at several layers and must be modeled separately from availability.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom publishes concrete capacity controls including 2,000 users per queue, up to 100 concurrent emails, 20 messaging engagements and 200 work items per agent, plus explicit API rate limits.

claims.Buyer_Implication: Architecture offers strong surge/failover evidence, but load-test/contract proof remains required.
claims.Publishable_Summary: Zoom's active-active SIP-zone design targets no more than 50% utilization in each zone during normal operations, creating architectural failover headroom; this does not establish unlimited buyer-specific concurrency.

breaks.Affected_Buyer_or_Use_Case: Desk-phone-centric operations, branch/service desks, certain regulated or operational environments with physical-phone workflows.
breaks.Build_or_Config_Implication: Endpoint redesign, device/workflow retraining and possibly split-platform telephony.
breaks.Buyer_Question: Can every required agent persona use a supported Zoom Contact Center endpoint without a physical IP phone dependency?
breaks.Change_Consequence: Future endpoint policy changes require regression across agent UX and telephony.
breaks.Cost_Consequence: Can add endpoint change, training, coexistence or alternate-platform cost.
breaks.Day2_Consequence: Mixed endpoint estate or user workflow change persists after go-live.
breaks.Exit_Point: Select another architecture for the affected agent population if physical IP-phone operation is mandatory.
breaks.Mitigation_Method: Redesign the agent endpoint around supported Zoom Workplace desktop/web/VDI/CTI endpoints or retain another voice/control path for the affected population.
breaks.Refresh_Trigger: Zoom adds supported IP-phone agent handling or materially changes endpoint architecture.
breaks.Trigger_Condition: The buyer requires contact-center agents to handle Zoom Contact Center engagements from physical IP phones rather than supported Zoom Workplace/web/CTI endpoints.

breaks.Affected_Buyer_or_Use_Case: Multi-client BPOs using pooled/shared agents across programs.
breaks.Break_Summary: BPO shared-agent model conflicts with ZCX Division isolation
breaks.Build_or_Config_Implication: May require duplicated users/workspaces, separate accounts or less-efficient staffing architecture.
breaks.Buyer_Question: Show a live agent serving two isolated client programs without breaking division isolation, reporting, WFM, recording or policy boundaries.
breaks.Change_Consequence: Client staffing changes may require user moves that can remove division-specific configuration and interrupt work.
breaks.Cost_Consequence: Reduced labor pooling efficiency, duplicated administration and possible license/account overhead.
breaks.Day2_Consequence: Program moves and cross-client staffing become governed admin events rather than seamless agent switching.
breaks.Exit_Point: Choose another tenancy/staffing architecture if shared-agent economics are mandatory and dedicated client pools are unacceptable.
breaks.Mitigation_Method: Use dedicated client agent pools, separate accounts/tenants, or redesign staffing so each user remains assigned to one division at a time.
breaks.Refresh_Trigger: ZCX Divisions changes user membership, cross-division agent behavior or tenancy model.
breaks.Trigger_Condition: A BPO needs one agent to work multiple client programs/divisions concurrently while retaining hard client isolation.

breaks.Affected_Buyer_or_Use_Case: Public sector, regulated financial/healthcare, sovereign-cloud or strict data-locality deployments.
breaks.Build_or_Config_Implication: Requires region/service-boundary selection, data-flow mapping and possibly separate environments.
breaks.Buyer_Question: Map persistent content, service/diagnostic data, media, AI inference, subprocessors and support access by country for the exact SKU/region.
breaks.Change_Consequence: New AI/model/channel features can re-open locality review.
breaks.Cost_Consequence: Can add separate environments, reduced feature choice, legal review and operating duplication.
breaks.Day2_Consequence: Continuous review of regional service, AI provider and subprocessor changes.
breaks.Exit_Point: Eliminate the proposed Zoom service path if a mandatory locality requirement cannot be contractually proven.
breaks.Mitigation_Method: Select the appropriate region-specific account/government environment, constrain features/providers, document subprocessors, or redesign workload scope.
breaks.Refresh_Trigger: Region, SIP-zone, government-service, AI-provider or subprocessor change.
breaks.Trigger_Condition: The buyer requires data, media and AI processing to remain within a jurisdiction or approved region that does not align with the selected Zoom account/SIP-zone/model-provider path.

breaks.Affected_Buyer_or_Use_Case: Large enterprise, bursty digital programs, automation-heavy integrations, high-scale BPO or event-driven service.
breaks.Break_Summary: Buyer topology exceeds documented queue/API/agent capacity controls
breaks.Build_or_Config_Implication: Topology and integration redesign plus load/failure testing.
breaks.Buyer_Question: Demonstrate our peak mix against queue, agent concurrency, API and failover limits with measured headroom.
breaks.Change_Consequence: Growth or automation can force queue/API redesign.
breaks.Cost_Consequence: Additional engineering, test, observability and potential architectural segmentation.
breaks.Day2_Consequence: Capacity monitoring and rate-limit governance become ongoing obligations.
breaks.Exit_Point: Select another topology/platform if required peak cannot be supported with acceptable headroom and operational complexity.
breaks.Mitigation_Method: Shard queues/workloads, redesign API patterns, use backoff/batching, request architecture review and prove failover headroom.
breaks.Refresh_Trigger: Published capacity limits, rate limits or SIP-zone architecture change.
breaks.Trigger_Condition: Required queue membership, per-agent digital concurrency, API transaction rates or failover load exceed documented limits/headroom.

breaks.Affected_Buyer_or_Use_Case: Complex enterprise transformation beyond packaged Zoom/CRM patterns.
breaks.Break_Summary: Unified-stack simplicity erodes under bespoke enterprise orchestration
breaks.Build_or_Config_Implication: More discovery, integration engineering, regression, governance and services than the initial simplification thesis suggests.
breaks.Buyer_Question: What percentage of our target architecture remains standard Zoom configuration versus custom cross-platform engineering?
breaks.Change_Consequence: Custom logic increases dependency on API/release/model governance.
breaks.Cost_Consequence: Transformation and Day-2 labor can materially exceed the license simplification benefit.
breaks.Day2_Consequence: More admin/API/AI/telephony surfaces and shared incident ownership.
breaks.Exit_Point: Use a broader process/control-plane architecture or narrow Zoom scope if the buyer cannot sustain the bespoke Day-2 model.
breaks.Mitigation_Method: Keep durable business state in CRM/BPM/SOR, narrow custom scope, use packaged integrations where possible and define authority/RACI boundaries.
breaks.Ownership_During_Implementation: Enterprise architect / SI / Zoom professional services
breaks.Refresh_Trigger: Material Zoom CX architecture, migration tooling, integration, AI or services-model change.
breaks.Trigger_Condition: A buyer selects Zoom for simplicity then expands scope into complex legacy migration, highly bespoke CRM/process state, BYOC, strict sovereignty, deep WEM transformation or high-authority agentic transactions.
